# Baudrillard — Fatal Strategies (1983)

## Bibliographic identity

French original: *Les Stratégies fatales* (Paris: Grasset, 1983). The [consulted primary scan-text carrier](https://www.scribd.com/document/603774005/Jean-Baudrillard-Fatal-Strategies-Semiotext-e-2008-1) identifies the **2008 Semiotext(e)** edition, ISBN 9781584350613, with Dominic Pettman's introduction. Its title credits Philippe Beitchman and W. G. J. Niesluchowski (OCR corrupts the latter ending). Earlier 1990 publication remains separate;2008 page numbers are not 1990 locators. Pettman's “A Belated Invitation to the Orgy” is an introduction, not Baudrillard's main text or the opening of Forget Foucault.

**Full note:** Jean Baudrillard, *Fatal Strategies*, trans. Philippe Beitchman and W. G. J. Niesluchowski, introduction by Dominic Pettman (Los Angeles: Semiotext(e), 2008), 219–30.

**Shortened note:** Baudrillard, *Fatal Strategies*, page.

**Bibliography:** Baudrillard, Jean. *Fatal Strategies*. Translated by Philippe Beitchman and W. G. J. Niesluchowski. Introduction by Dominic Pettman. Los Angeles: Semiotext(e), 2008.

## Source scholarship

The closing chapter places fatal theory on the side of an object whose response can exceed the subject's intended game. It also questions whether a fatal strategy can be secured as a strategy at all. This resists the intake's conversion into instructions for a subject to accelerate collapse. Yet the correction must retain the text's extremity: pp.222–25 develops worsening, spectacle and the deepening of negative conditions. Anti-programmatic does not mean moderate or conciliatory.

The lens may test an account's claim to master its object through this difference. Baudrillard's object and native Bimba retain distinct ontological offices. His speculation about nuclear spectacle is not an empirical safety guarantee.
